title: ICU: The High-Pressure Alarm
intro: A 60-year-old on volume control for pneumonia sets off the high-pressure alarm repeatedly. A new nurse wants to raise the alarm limit so it stops sounding.

decisions.prompt: The alarm sounds again. What is your first step?

options.text: Silence it and check the ventilator settings
options.explain: Silencing an alarm without finding the cause is the most dangerous action in critical care.
The limit shouldn't be raised without justification; it's set 10–15 cm H₂O above the observed PIP.
Correct. Alarm → patient → ventilator → cause → fix.
options.src: What is the first step when any ventilator alarm sounds?

decisions.prompt: PIP has risen from 30 to 45 cm H₂O; Pplat is unchanged at 25. Likely cause?

options.explain: Correct. High PIP with an unchanged Pplat is a resistance problem — when only PIP moves, think airways.
options.src: PIP rose from 30 to 45 cm H₂O; Pplat is unchanged at 25. What is the likely cause?

options.explain: Stiffer lungs raise Pplat too. Here Pplat hasn't moved.
A leak LOWERS pressures; it doesn't raise them.

decisions.prompt: Low exhaled VT and high-pressure alarms are now sounding together. This is:

options.explain: Low volume with LOW pressure is a leak.
Correct. Low volume + high pressure = obstruction. Drain condensate, replace the HME, suction.
options.src: The low exhaled VT and high pressure alarms sound together. What is the problem?

options.explain: Two alarms together always need a cause found.

decisions.prompt: After suctioning, PIP and Pplat both jump by 15 and breath sounds vanish on the left. Suspect:

options.text: A larger mucus plug lower in the airway
options.explain: A plug raises PIP; a sudden rise in BOTH PIP and Pplat with one-sided silence is a compliance problem.
Bronchospasm raises PIP with Pplat unchanged and causes wheezing, not silence.
Correct. Both pressures up suddenly with absent breath sounds on one side = tension pneumothorax or a mainstem tube.
options.src: PIP and Pplat both rise suddenly by 15 cm H₂O and breath sounds disappear on one side. What should the RT suspect?

decisions.prompt: Once that's fixed, his Pplat stays above 30 on volume control. Per Heuer:

options.text: Switch to pressure control with a limit ≤ 30
options.explain: Correct. Switch VC → PC when Pplat exceeds 30, using a pressure limit of 30 or less.
options.src: When should a patient be switched from VC to PC per Heuer?

options.text: Raise the tidal volume to improve ventilation
options.explain: More volume raises Pplat further and risks lung injury.

options.text: Accept any Pplat if the SpO₂ is good
options.explain: Pplat above 30 risks ventilator-induced lung injury, regardless of the SpO₂.

title: ICU: Ready to Come Off?
intro: A 55-year-old has been ventilated for 5 days for pneumonia, which is improving. She's on FiO₂ 0.40 and PEEP 5, with a P/F of 220. The team asks whether she's ready to wean.

decisions.prompt: Do her oxygenation numbers meet the criteria to begin a weaning assessment?

options.text: No — PEEP must be zero and FiO₂ 0.21 first
options.explain: PEEP up to 5–8 is acceptable for starting a weaning assessment.
Correct. She meets them, along with reversal of the cause and hemodynamic stability.
options.src: Which oxygenation criteria must be met to begin a weaning assessment?

options.text: No — she needs P/F above 400 on room air
options.explain: That's normal lung function, not the weaning threshold.

decisions.prompt: Off the vent she breathes at 38/min with a VT of 300 mL. RSBI?

options.explain: Correct. 38 ÷ 0.3 = 127, above 105.
options.src: A patient breathes spontaneously at 38/min with a VT of 300 mL. What is the RSBI, and what does it predict?

options.explain: The math is right, but above 105 predicts failure.
RSBI is rate ÷ VT in liters: 38 ÷ 0.3, not 300 ÷ 38.

decisions.prompt: She fails the SBT. What happens next?

options.text: Try the SBT again in another 30 minutes
options.explain: Repeated SBTs the same day just fatigue her muscles.

options.text: Extubate anyway and put her on BiPAP
options.explain: A failed SBT means she isn't ready to be extubated.

options.text: Full support, fix the cause, retry in 24 hr
options.explain: Correct. Rest her on full support, look for the cause, and repeat the SBT every 24 hours.
options.src: A patient fails an SBT. What happens next?

decisions.prompt: Two days later she passes. Which number shows she can clear secretions after extubation?

options.text: MEP ≥ 20 cm H₂O or cough flow ≥ 10 L/min
options.explain: Those values are far too weak to clear secretions.

options.text: MEP ≥ 60 cm H₂O or peak cough flow ≥ 60 L/min
options.explain: Correct. Heuer's extubation thresholds for an alert patient: MEP above 60 or peak cough flow above 60 L/min.
options.src: What MEP or peak cough flow indicates adequate secretion clearance before extubation?

options.text: MIP of −10 cm H₂O on a one-way valve
options.explain: A MIP of −10 is critically weak, and MIP measures inspiratory, not cough, strength.

decisions.prompt: Right after extubation she develops inspiratory stridor. Recommend:

options.text: Cool humidified O₂ and racemic epinephrine
options.explain: Correct. Keep racemic epinephrine available at every extubation.
options.src: Stridor develops right after extubation. What should the RT recommend?

options.text: A bronchodilator MDI, and nothing else for now
options.explain: Stridor is upper-airway swelling; a bronchodilator targets the lower airways.
Treat the swelling first; reintubate only if it fails.

title: ED Triage: Night Sweats and Bloody Sputum
intro: A 41-year-old reports weeks of low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and a cough now bringing up bloody sputum. The chest film shows upper-lobe cavitation.

decisions.prompt: This picture suggests:

options.explain: Correct. Low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and bloody sputum suggest reactivation TB.
options.src: Which set of symptoms suggests REACTIVATION (active) TB?

options.explain: Latent TB is walled off, has no symptoms and isn't infectious.
Weeks of night sweats, weight loss and cavitation aren't influenza.

decisions.prompt: Which room does he need?

options.text: A semi-private room with the curtain drawn
options.explain: TB is airborne. A curtain doesn't contain droplet nuclei.

options.text: A positive-pressure room with HEPA-filtered supply air
options.explain: Positive pressure pushes contaminated air OUT of the room.
Correct. Negative pressure pulls air in so contaminated air can't escape. Keep the door closed.
options.src: What room is required for a patient on AIRBORNE precautions?

decisions.prompt: What respiratory protection do you wear?

options.text: A surgical mask whenever within 3 feet
options.explain: A surgical mask is for DROPLET precautions. TB needs an N95.

options.text: A fit-tested N95, seal-checked each time
options.explain: Correct. Fit-tested NIOSH N95 with a user-seal check every time (or a PAPR).
options.src: What respiratory protection must the RT wear for a patient on airborne precautions?

options.text: No mask at all if he is wearing one
options.explain: Airborne precautions protect the RT regardless of the patient's mask.

decisions.prompt: How many sputum samples for AFB?

options.explain: Correct. 3 samples over 8–24 hours, each 5 mL or more of deep lung secretions; saliva isn't acceptable.
options.src: How many sputum samples are collected for AFB testing?

options.explain: One sample misses too many cases.
Too few, and not including an early-morning sample.

decisions.prompt: During sputum induction his FEV₁ falls 22% from baseline. You:

options.explain: A fall of 20% or more is the stop point.
Correct. Stop if FEV₁ falls 20% or more; pretreat reactive-airway patients with a fast-acting β-agonist.
options.src: During sputum induction, the FEV₁ falls 22% from baseline. What should the RT do?

options.text: Switch to 10% saline to finish faster
options.explain: Stronger saline worsens the bronchospasm.

title: Transport: Oxygen to CT and Back
intro: A patient on a 40% air-entrainment mask needs a CT scan across the hospital. You grab an E cylinder reading 1500 psi.

decisions.prompt: At 4 L/min, how long will the E cylinder last?

options.src: An E cylinder reads 1500 psi at 4 L/min. How long will it last?

options.explain: That would need an H cylinder's 3.14 factor.
Check the math: 1500 × 0.28 = 420 L, ÷ 4 L/min = 105 minutes.

decisions.prompt: The scanner often runs late. How much O₂ should you carry?

options.text: Exactly enough for the one-way trip to CT
options.explain: Delays are common. Running out mid-scan is a disaster.

options.text: At least twice the volume needed for a one-way trip
options.explain: Correct. The transport deck says the E cylinder must be full and carry at least twice the one-way volume.
options.src: For a transport with a possible delay, how much O₂ should be carried?

options.text: Whatever is left, since CT has wall oxygen
options.explain: You can't count on access to wall O₂ along the way or during delays.

decisions.prompt: Her inspiratory demand is about 40 L/min. Does a 40% mask at 8 L/min meet it?

options.explain: Correct. 40% = 3:1, so 4 parts × 8 = 32 L/min, below 40. Raise the input to 12 L/min.
options.src: A 40% air-entrainment mask is set at 8 L/min. Does it meet a 40 L/min inspiratory demand?

options.explain: 48 L/min is a 35% mask (5:1). At 40% the ratio is 3:1.

options.text: Yes — any Venturi mask meets demand
options.explain: At higher FiO₂ settings, less air is entrained, so total flow can fall short.

decisions.prompt: On return she needs 70% O₂ with a high flow demand. Best approach?

options.explain: At 70%, 15 × 1.6 = 24 L/min — entrainment fails at high demand.
A simple mask can't deliver a reliable 70% at a high demand.

options.text: A blender system or heated HFNC
options.explain: Correct. Above 0.60 with a high demand, entrainment fails; use a blender or heated high-flow cannula.
options.src: A patient needs 70% O₂ with a high inspiratory flow demand. Which is the best approach?

decisions.prompt: She turns out to have COPD with chronic CO₂ retention. What SpO₂ do you target?

options.explain: Excess FiO₂ can worsen hypercapnia in a retainer.
Correct. COPD target 88–92%; Venturi masks and HFNC give precise FiO₂ control.
options.src: What is the SpO₂ target in COPD?

options.explain: Too low — that's significant hypoxemia.

title: Code Blue: Watching the Capnogram
intro: A 66-year-old collapses on the medical floor. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. CPR is underway and you're managing the airway.

decisions.prompt: How is his VF treated?

options.explain: Correct. Biphasic 120–200 J (monophasic 360 J), then epinephrine and amiodarone or lidocaine.
options.src: How is ventricular fibrillation treated?

options.explain: Cardioversion needs an organized rhythm with a pulse. Pulseless VF needs defibrillation.

options.text: CPR and epinephrine only — no shock
options.explain: That's for non-shockable rhythms (PEA, asystole). VF is shockable.

decisions.prompt: He's intubated. What is the gold standard to confirm tube placement?

options.text: Equal breath sounds on both sides
options.explain: Breath sounds can mislead, especially during CPR.
Fogging also occurs with esophageal placement.
Correct. Esophageal intubation gives no CO₂ waveform.
options.src: What is the gold standard for confirming tracheal tube placement?

decisions.prompt: During compressions the PetCO₂ reads 8 mm Hg. This means:

options.explain: Correct. Below 10 reflects poor pulmonary blood flow — push harder and faster, switch compressors.
options.src: During CPR, a PetCO₂ below 10 mm Hg indicates:

options.text: The tube is in the esophagus
options.explain: Esophageal placement gives NO waveform at all, not a low one.
During arrest, a low PetCO₂ reflects low blood flow, not overventilation.

decisions.prompt: After a shock, the PetCO₂ suddenly rises from 12 to 38 mm Hg. This suggests:

options.explain: Correct. A sudden jump in PetCO₂ during CPR signals ROSC.
options.src: During CPR, PETCO₂ suddenly rises from 12 to 38 mm Hg. What does this suggest?

options.text: A disconnection in the breathing circuit
options.explain: A disconnection drops PetCO₂ to zero.
Poor CPR LOWERS PetCO₂.

title: ICU Day 4: Preventing VAP
intro: A 72-year-old is on day 4 of mechanical ventilation after abdominal surgery. On rounds, you review his VAP bundle and his recent trends.

decisions.prompt: He's lying almost flat. To what angle should the head of bed be raised?

options.explain: Correct. HOB 30–45° unless contraindicated (e.g., after neurosurgery, severe hypotension).
options.src: To what angle should the head of the bed be elevated to prevent VAP?

options.explain: Too flat to reduce microaspiration.
Supine positioning raises VAP risk.

decisions.prompt: Which suction system does the AARC endorse to reduce VAP?

options.text: Open suction with a sterile kit each time
options.explain: Open suction breaks the circuit.
He's intubated; nasotracheal suction isn't the issue.
Correct. Closed suction means the circuit is never broken.
options.src: Which suction system does the AARC endorse to reduce VAP?

decisions.prompt: Per the deck, what is the single best way to prevent VAP?

options.explain: Routine circuit changes don't prevent VAP and can add contamination.
Correct. Extubate as early as it is safe.
options.src: According to the deck, what is the single best way to prevent VAP?

options.explain: Prophylactic antibiotics aren't part of VAP prevention.

decisions.prompt: He develops a fever, rising WBC, purulent sputum and a new infiltrate. These findings:

options.explain: Correct. New or progressive infiltrates plus fever, high WBC and purulent sputum raise suspicion.
options.src: Which findings raise suspicion of VAP?

options.explain: A new infiltrate with fever and purulent sputum needs investigation.
These are exactly the findings that suggest it.

decisions.prompt: What confirms VAP?

options.text: A new infiltrate on the chest film, on its own
options.explain: Infiltrates raise suspicion but don't confirm the organism.

options.text: A fever above 38.5 °C lasting more than 2 days
options.explain: Fever alone doesn't confirm VAP.

options.text: A pathogen from a lower-airway sample taken before antibiotics
options.explain: Correct. BAL, protected brush, mini-BAL or an endotracheal aspirate — taken before starting or changing antibiotics.
options.src: What CONFIRMS VAP?
